name: Keyword Casing
description: Enforces consistent keyword casing (uppercase/lowercase/camelcase/consistent)
explanation:
Enforces consistent casing for TM1 keywords (IF, ENDIF, ELSE, ELSEIF, WHILE, END).

Supported styles:
- uppercase: IF, ENDIF, ELSE, WHILE, END
- lowercase: if, endif, else, while, end
- camelcase: If, Endif, Else, While, End
- consistent: Auto-detect from first keyword and enforce consistency
config_example:
rules:
  keyword_casing:
    enabled: true
    style: uppercase  # or lowercase, camelcase, consistent
default_config:
rules:
  keyword_casing:
    enabled: true
    severity: error
    style: uppercase

examples.description: uppercase style
lowercase style
Mixed casing

name: Whitespace Around Operators
description: Enforces exactly one space around binary operators
explanation: Every binary operator (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `<>`, `@=`, `@<>`, `&`, `|`) must have exactly one space on each side.  Unary operators (e.g. a leading `-1`) are exempt.  Operators at the start or end of a physical line are also exempt.
default_config:
rules:
  whitespace:
    enabled: true
    severity: error
    around_operators: true
    after_comma: true
    no_space_before_semicolon: true
    one_space_inside_parentheses: true
    no_multiple_spaces: true
    no_trailing_whitespace: true

examples.description: Missing spaces around operators

name: Whitespace After Comma
description: Enforces exactly one space after commas
explanation: Every comma must be followed by exactly one space.  Commas at the end of a physical line (multi-line argument lists) are exempt.
default_config:
rules:
  whitespace:
    enabled: true
    severity: error
    around_operators: true
    after_comma: true
    no_space_before_semicolon: true

    no_multiple_spaces: true
    no_trailing_whitespace: true

name: No Space Before Semicolon
description: Enforces no whitespace immediately before ';'
explanation: A semicolon that terminates a statement must not be preceded by any whitespace.  Only a semicolon at the start of a physical line (after a newline) is exempt.

    no_trailing_whitespace: true

name: One Space Inside Parentheses
description: Enforces exactly one space inside '(' and ')'
explanation: There must be exactly one space after an opening parenthesis and before a closing parenthesis.  Empty parentheses and multi-line parenthesised expressions (where the content starts on a new line) are exempt.

rules:

description: Enforces no multiple consecutive spaces (except indentation)
explanation: Two or more consecutive spaces are not allowed, except at the start of a line (indentation).  Use exactly one space between tokens.

explanation: Lines must not end with whitespace characters.  Trailing spaces or tabs before a newline (or at end of file) will be removed.

name: Block Indentation
description: Enforces indentation for IF/WHILE blocks and wrapped lines
explanation:
Enforces consistent indentation for IF and WHILE blocks.
The default indentation size is 4 spaces per nesting level. This can be configured via the `size` parameter.

A line that continues a statement started earlier — a wrapped argument list, a multi-line condition — is indented in the *hanging* style: one level deeper per open parenthesis, and the line that closes a parenthesis returns to the level of the line that opened it. Set `continuation_style` to `aligned` to line wrapped content up under the opening parenthesis instead, or to `ignore` to leave hand-formatted continuation lines alone.

Lines inside a multi-line string literal are never touched: their indentation is part of the string's value.
config_example:
rules:
  indentation:
    enabled: true
    size: 4  # number of spaces per indentation level
    continuation_style: hanging  # hanging | aligned | ignore
default_config:
rules:
  indentation:
    enabled: true
    severity: error
    size: 4
    continuation_style: hanging

examples.description: 4-space indent
Wrapped argument list (hanging indent)
Missing indentation
Wrapped line not at the hanging indent

name: One Statement Per Line
description: Enforces that each statement is followed by a newline
explanation:
Enforces that after a completed statement (marked by a semicolon), code continues on a new line.

Exception: no newline is required when the statement is immediately before the procedure end (EOF).
default_config:
rules:
  newline_per_statement:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

examples.description: Each statement on its own line
Multiple statements on same line

name: Maximum Line Length
description: Limits how long a physical line may be
explanation:
Flags any physical line longer than `limit` characters (120 by default).

The fix rewraps the statement across several lines, breaking at the commas of an argument list or before the operators of a long condition, and indenting the result in the hanging style F310 enforces.  Long comment lines are wrapped at word boundaries, preserving the leading ``#`` prefix on each continuation line.

Some long lines cannot be broken — a single long string literal, or a statement containing a comment that would change meaning if it moved. Those are reported without a fix.
default_config:
rules:
  max_line_length:
    enabled: true
    severity: error
    limit: 120
    indent_size: 4

examples.description: Wrapped at the argument boundaries
Wrapped before each operator

name: Variable Prefix Naming
description: Enforces TM1 variable naming conventions (n/s/c prefixes)
explanation:
Enforces TM1 variable naming conventions:
- Numeric variables must start with 'n': nCount, nValue, nSum
- String variables must start with 's': sMessage, sName, sPath
- Optional constants may start with 'c': cRate, cMessage

If `allow_constant_prefix` is enabled, any variable starting with 'c' may only be assigned once in the process (see C220).

If `allow_loop_counter_variables` is enabled, single-character numeric variables (e.g. i, j) that are assigned directly before a WHILE loop are exempt from naming conventions.

TM1 predefined system variables (e.g. DatasourceASCIIDecimalSeparator, NValue, SValue) are automatically excluded from naming convention checks.
config_example:
rules:
  variable_prefix:
    enabled: true
    allow_constant_prefix: false
    allow_loop_counter_variables: true
default_config:
rules:
  variable_prefix:
    enabled: true
    severity: error
    allow_constant_prefix: false
    allow_loop_counter_variables: false

name: Variables Consistent Casing
description: Enforces consistent casing for variable references within a process
explanation:
TM1 variables are case-insensitive, meaning `vYear`, `vyear`, and `VYEAR` all refer to the same variable. While technically valid, inconsistent casing reduces readability and breaks PAW variable highlighting when navigating code.

For parameters and data source variables, the casing from the metadata declaration is used as the canonical form. For script variables, the first occurrence in code defines the canonical casing.

The autofix replaces all inconsistent references with the canonical form.
default_config:
rules:
  variable_consistent_casing:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

Inconsistent casing for the same variable

name: Parameter Naming
description: Enforces that parameters start with lowercase 'p'
explanation:
Enforces that TM1 process parameters start with lowercase 'p'.

Parameters are the input values defined in the YAML Parameters section of a TM1 TI process. Following a consistent naming convention makes it easy to identify parameters throughout the code.
default_config:
rules:
  parameter_naming:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

name: Data Source Variable Naming
description: Enforces that data source variables start with lowercase 'v'
explanation:
Enforces that TM1 data source variables start with lowercase 'v'.

Data source variables are the columns from the data source, defined in the YAML Variables section. These variables are automatically populated by TM1 during Metadata and Data processing.
default_config:
rules:
  variable_naming:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

name: Docstring Region
description: Enforces a docstring region before executable code in the prolog
explanation: Every process prolog must begin with a ``#Region - Docstring`` section (name is configurable) that appears before any executable statement (i.e. before the first ``;``). The region must contain at least a ``# Description`` header. Processes whose names start with a configured *generic prefix* (e.g. ``}core.``) must also contain the extra headers defined in ``generic_extra_headers``.
config_example:
rules:
  docstring_region:
    enabled: true
    region_name: Docstring
    required_headers:
      - '# Description'
    generic_prefixes:
      - '}core.'
    generic_extra_headers:
      - '# Use Case'
default_config:
rules:
  docstring_region:
    enabled: false
    severity: error
    region_name: Docstring
    required_headers:
    - '# Description'
    generic_prefixes: []
    generic_extra_headers:
    - '# Use Case'

examples.code:
#Region - Docstring
# Description:
# Does something useful
#EndRegion - Docstring
nVar = 1;

name: Empty Block
description: Flags IF/ELSEIF/ELSE/WHILE blocks that contain no executable code
explanation:
Flags control-flow blocks (IF/ELSEIF/ELSE/WHILE) that contain no executable code, either because they are completely empty or because they hold only comments.

Auto-fix removes a block only when it is completely empty (no comments) and deletion is safe: an empty ELSE, an empty WHILE (including its END;), or an empty ELSEIF that is the last branch. An empty ELSEIF followed by another ELSEIF/ELSE is reported only — removing it would change behaviour — as is any empty IF or any block that still holds a comment.
default_config:
rules:
  empty_block:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

Empty ELSE block (auto-fixable: branch removed)
Empty IF block
WHILE block with only a comment

name: Conditional Control Flow
description: Enforces that flow-altering statements are only used inside an IF/ELSE block
explanation:
Enforces that flow-altering control statements are only used inside an IF/ELSE block.

The following functions and keywords abruptly change process flow and must be guarded by an explicit IF condition:
- ProcessQuit
- ItemReject
- ProcessBreak
- ProcessError
- ProcessExitByChoreRollback
- ProcessExitByProcessRollback
- ProcessRollback
- Break

Using any of them in the main program body — or in a bare WHILE loop with no enclosing IF — is almost always a logic error.
default_config:
rules:
  conditional_control_flow:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

name: ItemSkip Block Usage
description: Enforces that ItemSkip() is only used in metadata or data sections
explanation:
Deprecated: use Invalid Function Placement (C150), configured via rules.misplaced_function. This rule remains available with its original ItemSkip-only behavior, but is disabled by default and is skipped with a warning whenever C150 is active, so the same ItemSkip is never reported twice. Selecting C130 (or its alias S120) explicitly still runs it.

Enforces that ItemSkip() is only used in metadata or data sections of TM1 TI processes.

TM1 TI processes have four execution blocks:
- Prolog: Executes once before processing records
- Metadata: Processes dimension metadata records
- Data: Processes cube data records
- Epilog: Executes once after all records

ItemSkip() skips the current record, which only makes sense in Metadata and Data sections. Using it in Prolog or Epilog is a logic error.
config_example:
rules:
  item_skip:
    # Deprecated: prefer rules.misplaced_function (C150), which
    # takes precedence whenever both rules are active.
    enabled: true
default_config:
rules:
  item_skip:
    enabled: false
    severity: error

examples.description: ItemSkip in Metadata/Data
ItemSkip in Prolog

name: Unreachable Code
description: Flags code after a flow-terminating statement that can never execute
explanation:
Flags unreachable code that follows a flow-terminating statement within a block.

Statements such as ProcessQuit, ProcessBreak, ProcessError, ItemReject, the ProcessRollback family and the Break loop keyword end the current flow. A flow-terminating statement must therefore be the last statement in its block; anything after it can never execute.
default_config:
rules:
  unreachable_code:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

Unreachable code after ProcessQuit

name: Invalid Function Placement
description: Detects TI functions used in a procedure section where they are not allowed
explanation:
Checks function calls against the Prolog, Metadata, Data and Epilog sections and reports a placement the IBM function reference documents as invalid. Valid placement produces no diagnostic.

- DimensionElementInsert / HierarchyElementInsert: valid in Prolog/Metadata; invalid in Data/Epilog.
- DimensionElementComponentAdd / HierarchyElementComponentAdd: valid in Prolog/Metadata/Data; invalid in Epilog.
- DisableBulkLoadMode: valid in the Epilog; invalid in Prolog/Metadata/Data, because bulk load mode has to stay on for the whole process. IBM asks for it in the Epilog's last line; that position is not checked.
- AddInfoCubeRestriction: valid in the Prolog only (IBM: "must be placed in the Prolog").
- DisableMTQViewConstruct: invalid in Metadata/Data. IBM wants it in the Prolog, where it is the only place it has an effect, or, after EnableMTQViewConstruct, on the Epilog's last line; that position is not checked.
- Dimension and Hierarchy Direct functions: ElementInsertDirect, ElementDeleteDirect, ElementComponentAddDirect, ElementComponentDeleteDirect and TopElementInsertDirect are unrestricted in all four sections. IBM describes direct edits during Data loads; they do not inherit the non-Direct functions' restrictions.
- ItemSkip: valid in Metadata/Data; invalid in Prolog/Epilog.

Restrictions are function-specific. ElementDelete, ElementComponentDelete and TopElementInsert are not automatically restricted like ElementInsert. See docs/function-placement.md for the IBM sources.

Placements that are only discouraged (for example attribute writes in Metadata, security changes in Data/Epilog, once-per-process operations in Metadata/Data) are reported as warnings by Discouraged Function Placement (C151), which shares this rule's placement table. `--select C15` runs both. Before C151 existed, this rule reported those recommendations as errors; a `# noqa: C150` no longer suppresses them, use `# noqa: C151`.

Function matching is case-insensitive. Unknown functions and code without a known procedure section are not reported. Calls inside expressions and nested control flow are checked too. Statements the parser could not read are skipped.

allowed_functions lists functions to exempt from the check in every section, for a placement this project disagrees with. C151 falls back to this list when it sets none of its own.

Supersedes ItemSkip Block Usage (C130), which is disabled by default and skipped with a warning whenever this rule is active, so the same ItemSkip is never reported twice. Selecting C130 (or its alias S120) explicitly still runs the legacy ItemSkip-only rule with its own rules.item_skip settings.
config_example:
rules:
  misplaced_function:
    enabled: true
    # Functions to exempt from the placement check entirely.
    allowed_functions: []
default_config:
rules:
  misplaced_function:
    enabled: true
    severity: error
    report_not_recommended: true
    allowed_functions: []

name: Discouraged Function Placement
description: Warns about TI functions in a procedure section where they are allowed but discouraged
explanation:
Reports a placement that is allowed but recommended against. It shares the placement table of Invalid Function Placement (C150), which reports the documented restrictions as errors. `--select C15` runs both.

- AttrPutS / AttrPutN / ElementAttrPutS / ElementAttrPutN: discouraged in Metadata. Buffered dimension changes become visible only after the Metadata procedure finishes, so writing attributes in Data avoids referring to elements still being created. Updating elements that already exist can be intentional in Metadata. When the element is provably new, Element Used Before Available (C152) reports the concrete error instead of this warning.
- AddClient / DeleteClient / AddGroup / DeleteGroup / CellSecurityCubeCreate / CellSecurityCubeDestroy: discouraged in Data/Epilog. Their IBM references say that, like all functions that update metadata, they should not be used in the Data or Epilog tabs. Client and group changes take effect only after the Metadata procedure has finished.
- DimensionUpdateDirect / HierarchyUpdateDirect: discouraged in Metadata/Data. IBM: the call "incurs an initial full-copy memory cost", which these sections pay once per source record.
- DimensionDeleteAllElements / DimensionDeleteElements / HierarchyDeleteAllElements / HierarchyDeleteElements: valid in the Prolog only. Emptying a dimension per record or after the load discards what the process builds.
- Once-per-process operations, discouraged in Metadata/Data because they run once per source record: CubeClearData, ViewZeroOut, CubeProcessFeeders, SecurityRefresh, SaveDataAll, CubeSaveData, CubeCreate/Destroy, DimensionCreate/Destroy, HierarchyCreate/Destroy, ViewCreate/Destroy, ViewCreateByMDX, SubsetCreate/Destroy, SubsetCreateByMDX, RefreshMdxHierarchy, CubeSetLogChanges, EnableBulkLoadMode, ASCIIDelete, DimensionSortOrder, HierarchySortOrder.
- EnableMTQViewConstruct: discouraged in Metadata/Data. IBM: "You can enable EnableMTQViewConstruct in either the Prolog or Epilog section".
- SetInputCharacterSet: valid in the Prolog only. It describes the data source, which is opened when the Prolog ends.

The UpdateDirect, dimension-emptying and once-per-process entries are discouraged in Metadata/Data only because those sections repeat them per source record. A call inside an IF or ELSE body is not reported there when the condition can differ between records, because it then selects the records the call runs for (a header line, the first record). That needs a data source variable in the condition, or a variable Metadata or Data assign a value that is not provably constant, such as a record counter. A condition on parameters, constants or Prolog values is the same on every record and does not count. A call in the IF's own condition, or in a WHILE outside any IF, is still reported.

The security, UpdateDirect and MTQ entries rest on the IBM references; the others are LinTi recommendations. See docs/function-placement.md.

These recommendations used to be C150 errors. They are now warnings under their own ID, so a `# noqa: C150` no longer suppresses them; use `# noqa: C151`.

allowed_functions exempts functions in every section. Unless this rule sets its own list, it uses rules.misplaced_function.allowed_functions. The deprecated rules.misplaced_function.report_not_recommended: false switches this rule off as long as rules.discouraged_function_placement.enabled is not set.
config_example:
rules:
  discouraged_function_placement:
    enabled: true
    # Functions to exempt; unset falls back to
    # rules.misplaced_function.allowed_functions.
    allowed_functions: []
default_config:
rules:
  discouraged_function_placement:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
    allowed_functions: null

name: Element Used Before Available
description: Detects cube access to an element whose buffered insert is not yet available
explanation:
DimensionElementInsert and HierarchyElementInsert are buffered. The new element is in the dimension index at once, so DIMIX already finds it, but cubes, including }ElementAttributes_<dimension>, can address it only after the Metadata phase has ended. Until then an attribute write is lost and a read returns no value; the process only ends with minor errors.

The phase spans Prolog and Metadata: an element inserted in the Prolog is still unreachable in Metadata, on every source record. Once a buffered insert has run, an element inserted later in the same dimension is unreachable as well, even when a Direct insert created it. Elements that already existed are not affected.

The rule reports only what it can prove on one execution path:
- the element is new: the insert sits in an IF branch whose condition establishes DIMIX(dim, el) = 0 or ElementIndex(dim, hier, el) = 0 for the same element;
- the access targets the same dimension, hierarchy and element: equal literals, or the same variable not reassigned in between;
- the insert is pending on every path to the access. A path that ends first (ProcessQuit, ProcessError, ProcessBreak, ItemReject, ItemSkip, a rollback) does not count.

Checked writes: AttrPutS/N, ElementAttrPutS/N, and CellPutS/N to a }ElementAttributes_<dimension> cube. Checked reads: AttrS/N, ElementAttrS/N, and CellGetS/N from such a cube. Other cubes are skipped, because their dimension order is unknown. A Direct insert makes the element addressable at once, as long as no buffered insert into that dimension ran before it. Data and Epilog are fine, since the phase has ended by then.

For the same call this finding replaces the general Discouraged Function Placement (C151) warning. Suppressing it with `# noqa: C152` lets the C151 warning through again.

Fix it by moving the access to Data, or by inserting the element with the Direct variant, before any buffered insert into the dimension, if that fits the process.
default_config:
rules:
  element_used_before_available:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

name: Data Source Usage
description: Detects Metadata/Data code that never runs without a data source, and data sources nothing uses
explanation:
Metadata and Data run once per data source record. The rule compares the data source in effect when Prolog ends with the executable code in Metadata and Data. That data source is the one in the process properties, followed through statically provable Prolog assignments to DatasourceType, so a data source set up in Prolog counts like one in the properties.

- Code without data source: the effective data source is None, but Metadata or Data contains executable code, which is skipped. Reported once per process, at the first affected statement, naming every affected section.
- Unused data source: a data source is in effect, but Metadata and Data are both empty. Reported at the Prolog assignment to DatasourceType when there is one, else at the start of the process. A drill-through use (ReturnSQLTableHandle, ReturnViewHandle, ReturnCSVTableHandle) counts as use. Set check_unused_source: false to turn this finding off.
- Data source without variables: the process is saved without a data source and declares no variables, but Prolog turns one on by assigning DatasourceType while Metadata or Data contain code. The variables belong to the saved definition, so the records arrive with nothing to read their columns into, and tools that read the saved definition do not see the data source. Reported at the Prolog assignment. Save the process with its data source and variables, and keep Prolog for choosing which file, view or query it reads. Set check_runtime_source: false to turn this finding off.

Comments, blank lines and bare section markers count as empty; generated statements count as code. When the data source cannot be determined (a plain .ti file without process properties and without a provable Prolog assignment, a DatasourceType assigned from a parameter or inside a branch, or an unparseable Prolog statement mentioning DatasourceType), the rule stays silent. The fix is manual: move the code, set up the data source, or remove it.
config_example:
rules:
  data_source_usage:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
    # Set to false to drop the unused-data-source finding.
    check_unused_source: true
    # Set to false to drop the data-source-without-variables finding.
    check_runtime_source: true
default_config:
rules:
  data_source_usage:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
    check_unused_source: true
    check_runtime_source: true

name: Data Source Assigned After Prolog
description: Detects assignments to data source variables in Metadata, Data or Epilog
explanation:
IBM runs the Prolog before the data source is opened; Metadata and Data then process its records. Assigning a data source variable such as DatasourceQuery, DatasourceNameForServer or DatasourceType is how a process chooses its source at run time, and that only works in the Prolog. In Metadata, Data or Epilog the source has already been opened, so the assignment does not change what the process reads. A filtered query set in Data, for example, leaves the process loading the unfiltered original.

Checked variables are the data source variables of the IBM reference: DatasourceType, DatasourceNameForServer, DatasourceNameForClient, DatasourceQuery, DatasourceUsername, DatasourcePassword, DatasourceCubeview, DatasourceDimensionSubset, DatasourceJsonRootPointer and DatasourceJsonVariableMapping. Matching is case-insensitive. Reading them anywhere is fine.

The DatasourceASCII* settings are not checked: ASCIIOutput and TextOutput also use DatasourceASCIIDelimiter and DatasourceASCIIQuoteCharacter for the records they write, so setting them later to shape an export file is legitimate.

IBM documents the order, not the effect of a late assignment; that the assignment is ignored follows from it.

Fix it by moving the assignment into the Prolog.
default_config:
rules:
  data_source_assigned_after_prolog:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

name: Read-only Parameters and Variables
description: Enforces that parameters and data source variables are read-only
explanation:
Enforces that TM1 parameters and data source variables are read-only.

Parameters (from the Parameters section) and data source variables (from the Variables section) should not be modified in the process code. These values are inputs to your process and should be treated as immutable. If you need to change their values, assign them to a new local variable first.

Why this matters:
- Parameters represent user input or configuration values
- Variables represent data from the source that should be preserved
- Modifying these can make debugging difficult
- Following this convention makes code more readable and maintainable
default_config:
rules:
  readonly_parameter_variable:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

name: Single-assignment Constants
description: Enforces that constants (c-prefixed variables) are assigned only once
explanation:
Enforces that constants (variables starting with 'c') are assigned only once throughout the process.

This rule is automatically enabled when `allow_constant_prefix: true` is set in the variable_prefix rule.

    allow_constant_prefix: true  # Enables C220

name: Literal Process Calls
description: Enforces that RunProcess()/ExecuteProcess() use a string literal as first argument
explanation:
Enforces that RunProcess() and ExecuteProcess() calls use a string literal as their first argument (the target process name).

This keeps process lineage explicit and avoids dynamic indirection through variables/parameters.
default_config:
rules:

name: Use Hierarchy-Aware Functions
description: Enforces hierarchy-aware functions, or at least consistent usage of hierarchy-aware vs. standard hierarchy functions
explanation:
TM1 offers hierarchy-aware functions (e.g. HierarchyElementExists, ElementParent) that take an explicit hierarchy, alongside standard functions (e.g. DimensionElementExists, ELPAR) that implicitly use a dimension's default hierarchy.

Modes:
- enforce: only hierarchy-aware functions are allowed; standard functions are reported with their hierarchy-aware replacement.
- consistent: either style is allowed, but mixing both within the same file is reported.

Independently of the mode, a standard function whose dimension argument provably addresses a hierarchy ('Dimension:Hierarchy') is reported — whether the colon comes from a string literal, a literal concatenation (sDim | ':' | sHier), or a variable with a statically known branch variant that contains a colon (a single reachable path already addresses a hierarchy there, even if other branches don't). In enforce mode the call is already reported by name, so this extra check adds signal in consistent mode. Unknown/dynamic values are never reported.

Generic processes (whose names start with a configured ``generic_prefixes`` entry) are always held to the stricter ``enforce`` mode, regardless of the base ``mode``.

Covers both TI functions and Rules functions that are valid in TI.
config_example:
# Generic processes (top-level setting) are always enforced
generic_prefixes:
  - '}core.'
rules:
  use_hierarchy_aware_functions:
    enabled: true
    # base mode: 'enforce' or 'consistent'
    mode: consistent
default_config:
rules:
  use_hierarchy_aware_functions:
    enabled: true
    severity: error
    mode: consistent

examples.description: hierarchy-aware function (valid in any mode)
enforce mode: standard function (use HierarchyElementExists)
consistent mode: mixes hierarchy-aware and standard styles
dimension argument addresses a hierarchy; use HierarchyElementExists with an explicit hierarchy

name: Do Not Use Undocumented Functions
description: Reports calls to TurboIntegrator functions that are not officially documented or supported by IBM
explanation:
Some TI functions exist in the engine but are missing from IBM's documentation — for example DimensionElementInsertByAlias, LockOn or Hex. They are occasionally useful, but they come with no compatibility guarantee: behaviour can change or the function can vanish in any release, and IBM support does not cover them. Production code should rely on the documented API instead.

Matching is case-insensitive, and calls are found wherever they appear — including inside IF/WHILE conditions and nested arguments. Because TI makes the parentheses optional on a no-argument call, `LockOn;` is reported just like `LockOn();`. A name merely read as a variable is not a call and is never reported.

When the use is intentional, suppress the finding with a `# noqa: C430` comment on the line above (region- and procedure-level suppression works too), or list the function under `allowed_functions` to permit it across the whole project.
config_example:
rules:
  do_not_use_undocumented_functions:
    enabled: true
    # Functions the project knowingly relies on (case-insensitive):
    # allowed_functions:
    #   - DimensionElementInsertByAlias
default_config:
rules:
  do_not_use_undocumented_functions:
    enabled: true
    severity: error
    allowed_functions: []

name: Function Version Compatibility
description: Reports TurboIntegrator functions incompatible with a target Planning Analytics / TM1 version (v11, v12, or both)
explanation:
Some TI functions exist only in PA/TM1 v11 and are unsupported in v12; others were introduced in v12 and do not exist in v11. This rule reports calls that break a chosen compatibility target.

Modes:
- CompatibleWithV11AndV12: only functions available in both versions are allowed; any version-specific function is reported.
- V11: v11 functions are allowed; functions introduced in v12 are reported.
- V12: v12 functions are allowed; functions removed or unsupported in v12 are reported.

Matching is case-insensitive, and calls are found wherever they appear — including inside IF/WHILE conditions and nested arguments. Because TI makes the parentheses optional on a no-argument call, `SaveDataAll;` is reported just like `SaveDataAll();`.

The target version is normally set once via the top-level `target_version` (v11 | v12 | both) so other version-aware rules can share it; the per-rule `mode` overrides it when present.
config_example:
# Project-wide target, shared by version-aware rules:
target_version: both  # v11 | v12 | both
rules:
  function_version_compatibility:
    enabled: true
    # Optional per-rule override of target_version:
    # mode: CompatibleWithV11AndV12  # | V11 | V12
default_config:
rules:
  function_version_compatibility:
    enabled: false
    severity: error
    mode: null
    target_version: null

This ensures that sensitive credentials are managed through process parameters rather than hardcoded or undefined values.

2. Parameter name must start with 'p' (TI parameter naming convention)
3. Parameter must be declared in the process Parameters section

name: No Hardcoded Secrets
description: Reports variables whose name looks like a credential being fed from a hardcoded string literal or read out of a cube
explanation:
A credential written straight into the source ships with the process. Once the process is committed, the value is in version control for good — rotating it later does not remove it from the history. Pass secrets in as process parameters instead, so the value lives in the caller (or a secure store) rather than in the script.

Keeping the credential in a control cube and reading it back with CellGetS() is reported for the same reason. Cube values — attributes included, since they live in `}ElementAttributes_*` cubes — are held in the TM1 data directory. That directory *can* be encrypted, but in practice almost never is, so anyone with file access to the server, a backup or a snapshot reads the value without needing a TM1 login. Set `allow_secrets_in_cubes: true` if your deployment accepts that risk.

A variable is considered secret-looking when its name contains one of the configured fragments, matched case-insensitively (so `sPassword`, `vApiKey` and `sPwd_Prod` all qualify). It is reported when the value is provably a non-empty string — whether written directly, folded from a concatenation (`'let' | 'mein'`) or carried over from another variable that holds a literal — or when it comes from a direct cube read. For the most unambiguous fragments (`password`, `apikey`, `token`, ... — the `standard` preset) a numeric literal such as `sPassword = 12345;` counts too, since a PIN is still a hardcoded secret; the generic `strict`-only fragments (`key`, `auth`, `cert`, ...) and custom `secret_names` stay string-only, since those names are just as commonly an ordinary integer. Whatever cannot be resolved statically is left alone: parameters, datasource variables and other function results. So are half-known values such as `sPassword = 'prefix_' | pDyn;`, where the secret itself may well be dynamic, and the common `sPassword = '';` initialisation.

Neither the value nor the cube coordinates ever appear in linti's output — reports often end up in CI logs. Widen or narrow the name detection with `mode`, extend it with `secret_names`, or suppress a single finding with a `# noqa: X130` comment on the line above.
config_example:
rules:
  hardcoded_secret:
    enabled: true
    # relaxed | standard | strict | custom
    mode: standard
    # Extra name fragments (the whole list when mode is 'custom'):
    # secret_names:
    #   - kennwort
    # Set to true to accept credentials stored in a cube:
    allow_secrets_in_cubes: false
default_config:
rules:
  hardcoded_secret:
    enabled: true
    severity: error
    mode: standard
    secret_names: []
    allow_secrets_in_cubes: false

name: Filter ODBC Rows in SQL
description: Flags ItemSkip() or exclusively conditional writes in Metadata/Data when the ODBC data source query has no WHERE clause
explanation:
When an ODBC data source returns all rows and the filtering happens only in the TI script, the server pulls rows it immediately discards. This is reported in the Metadata and Data blocks when the data source query has no WHERE clause and either:
- ItemSkip() is used to skip records, or
- every cube write (CellPutN, CellPutS, CellIncrementN) is guarded by an IF, so no unconditional write ever happens.

Move the filter into a SQL WHERE clause so the database returns only the rows the process needs.

A DatasourceType/DatasourceQuery reassignment in the Prolog overrides the process metadata and is used instead.

Inspired by the Bedrock TM1 best practices (https://github.com/cubewise-code/bedrock).
default_config:
rules:
  sql_where_filtering:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

examples.datasource_query: SELECT region, amount, month FROM t

examples.description: ItemSkip() filters rows, no WHERE — filter in SQL
examples.datasource_query: SELECT region, amount, month FROM t

name: Unparseable Statement
description: Flags statements that could not be parsed, warning that linting quality is reduced for that code
explanation:
The parser could not understand this statement and kept it in the AST as an unknown statement so the rest of the section could still be linted. AST-based rules skip unknown statements entirely, so any problem inside one is never reported — linting quality is reduced there. Fixing the syntax (a missing semicolon, an unbalanced parenthesis, a stray token) restores full coverage.

This can equally mean linti's parser does not yet cover a construct TM1 accepts. If the process compiles on the server, it is a linti gap worth reporting — that is why this is a warning and does not fail a build by default.
config_example:
rules:
  unknown_statement:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
default_config:
rules:
  unknown_statement:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning

examples.description: A well-formed statement parses and is fully linted
Missing terminating semicolon — cannot be parsed

name: Trailing Comment
description: Flags trailing comments that follow code on the same line
explanation:
TI only allows a comment on a line of its own. A trailing comment after code on the same line (`nVar = 1; # note`) is saved by TM1 without an error, but the process fails when it runs.

This also applies to suppression comments: a trailing `# noqa: F220` has no effect, because linti only honours `noqa` directives on their own line.

The auto-fix moves the comment onto its own line directly above the code, with the same indentation, so a moved `# noqa` starts working for exactly that line. It is left to you when moving could change meaning: on a continuation line of a multi-line statement, for a `noqa-begin`/`noqa-end` marker (the region would shift), and for a `# noqa` on the first code line (it would turn into a procedure-wide suppression).
default_config:
rules:
  trailing_comment:
    enabled: true
    severity: error

examples.description: Comment on its own line
Trailing comment fails at runtime in TM1

name: Maximum Nesting Depth Exceeded
description: Flags a procedure whose statement or expression nesting exceeded the configured limit, stopping the parser before it could build a full AST for that section
explanation:
TI statements and expressions are parsed recursively; without a cap, pathologically deep nesting would recurse until Python's own RecursionError, crashing the run instead of reporting a clean diagnostic. `max_nesting_depth` (top-level config key, default 150) caps that recursion; once a procedure's nesting exceeds it, the parser aborts the section and this diagnostic reports the drop.

This safety cap itself cannot be turned off — only how loud linti is about hitting it. `rules.nesting_depth.enabled: false` silences the diagnostic, but the procedure is still dropped from linting exactly the same; the cap keeps applying either way. Raise `max_nesting_depth` if your codebase genuinely nests deeper than the default. Python stack exhaustion is also reported as P900.

Unlike every other rule, this diagnostic is enforced directly in the parser rather than by a rule module — there is nothing to `--select` or scan for in the AST, since the AST for the affected procedure was never built. Only `rules.nesting_depth.enabled` and `rules.nesting_depth.severity` control it.
config_example:
rules:
  nesting_depth:
    enabled: true    # hides the diagnostic only — the cap always applies
    severity: warning
default_config:
rules:
  nesting_depth:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
